15 A cyclist is travelling at a constant speed up a hill. The frictional force resisting the cyclist’s motion
is 8.0 N.
The cyclist uses 450 J of energy to travel a distance of 20 m.
What is the increase in the gravitational potential energy of the cyclist?
A
160 J
B
290 J
C
440 J
D
610 J

hints: Notice the cyclist moves at constant speed, so kinetic energy does not change and the 450 J must supply both friction work and gravitational potential energy.
Recall work against a constant resistive force is $W = Fd$ - calculate it for $8.0 \text{ N}$ over $20 \text{ m}$ in joules.
Subtract that friction energy from the total 450 J input to find what is left for the increase in $mgh$.
walkthrough: Constant speed up the hill means change in kinetic energy is zero, so the 450 J input is split into work against friction plus increase in gravitational potential energy.
Calculate work done against friction using $W = Fd$ with $F = 8.0 \text{ N}$ and $d = 20 \text{ m}$.
Substitution gives $W = 8.0 \times 20 = 160 \text{ J}$, with unit joules as $\text{N m}$.
Apply conservation: input energy = friction work + gain in potential energy, so gain = $450 - 160$.
Gain in gravitational potential energy = $290 \text{ J}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: 160 J is the work done against friction, $W = 8.0 \times 20$, not the energy left for gravitational potential energy.

B.explanation: After 160 J is lost to friction, $450 - 160 = 290$ J remains to increase gravitational potential energy at constant speed.

C.explanation: 440 J would leave only 10 J for friction, which does not match $8.0 \text{ N}$ over $20 \text{ m}$.

D.explanation: 610 J wrongly adds the friction work to 450 J instead of subtracting energy lost to friction.
